av_event.what: Before answering, Callum's smile drops and he looks away from the camera towards the window on his left for about three seconds, lips pressed together, then turns back to the screen.

text:
A: Hey! Hiya, can you hear me alright?
B: Hi! Yeah, hi, I'm Elira.
A: Callum. Birmingham.
B: Oh my God, Callum. Sorry, my boyfriend's called Callum, so this is going to be weird for me. Gary already asked if it was you.
A: Ha, no, I can confirm I'm not your boyfriend. What did Gary say about me?
B: Erm, he said you talked about his steel for ten minutes. And that you were a nice enough lad. Which I think from Gary is quite high praise?
A: Nice enough lad. I'll take that, honestly, I thought he hated me. I did go on about his beam a bit. He said six metres and my brain just went.
B: What do you do, then, that a beam does that to you?
A: Structural engineer. Graduate, so I'm doing the chartership thing. Mostly residential, concrete and steel frames. Basically I'm the person who tells the architect their lovely cantilever's not happening.
B: Ha, that sounds quite satisfying, though.
A: A bit too satisfying, apparently. It came up in my review. What about you, you're London, right?
B: Walthamstow, yeah. I'm between jobs, I took voluntary redundancy from a property management company, so I'm applying for office manager stuff. And doing a bookkeeping course. Sorry, I've said that sentence about five times today, it's starting to sound rehearsed.
A: Nah, it's fine. Property management, so you'd have had all the defects on the new-build blocks?
B: Oh, all of it. Damp, mostly. Every tenant ringing about damp, and the developer saying it's just people drying washing indoors.
A: Which, to be fair, is half of it. Ventilation's rubbish in loads of those blocks, you know? Trickle vents taped over, extractor fans that do nothing. I've got an airer in my spare room right now, so I'm part of the problem.
B: Ha, everyone is. Do you like Birmingham? I've only been once, for a wedding.
A: Love it, honestly. People sleep on it. I'm in Stirchley, it's all little bakeries and a brilliant wine shop now, it's basically turned into Walthamstow.
B: That's so funny, that's exactly what people say about Walthamstow. Would you ever move to London?
A: Er. Maybe. Some of the practices I'd love to work for are there. It's kind of a live conversation at home, Hannah's job's in Birmingham, so.
B: Oh, yeah, that's hard. And honestly, the rent alone, we pay a fortune for a one-bed above a shop.
A: What does your Callum do?
B: Sound technician, theatres and events. So he comes in at midnight after a get-out and I'm asleep. But he gets free tickets, so I've seen loads of musicals I'd never pay for.
A: Okay, what's the best one?
B: Erm, honestly, anything funny. I can't do the really heavy dramas, I just sit there wanting it to end. Is that bad?
A: No, that's fair. I'm the opposite, I drag Hannah to really slow films on Mubi and she falls asleep. Last one was a lighthouse keeper, three hours, barely any talking. It was overrated, to be fair, even I'll admit that.
B: Three hours! She deserves a medal. What do you do for fun that isn't a sad lighthouse?
A: Cooking, mostly. I've got a sourdough starter, Hannah named it Gerald. Fresh pasta at weekends. Five-a-side, and I'm getting back into bouldering after I did my finger.
B: Gerald! I love that. I'm trying to learn my mum's pite, it's an Albanian pastry, really thin layers. Mine always tears.
A: Is it like filo, rolled out by hand?
B: By hand, with a long thin rolling pin, my mum does it on the kitchen table. Mine ends up looking like a map.
A: Ha. It's probably the resting. You want the dough really soft and then leave it ages. Do you rest it?
B: Sorry, rest it how long?
A: Like an hour, under a bit of oil. Then it stretches instead of tearing, right?
B: I do about ten minutes. Okay, I'm telling my mum a man from Birmingham fixed her recipe.
A: Don't tell her that, she'll never forgive me.
